lesson.title: The Geometry of Straight Lines and the Angles They Make
lesson.summary: Lines and the angles formed where they meet or cross a third line follow a small, predictable set of relationships, and slope measures how steeply a line rises, both of which let you find missing angles and equations quickly.
lesson.body:
When two lines cross, they form angles with several fixed relationships worth knowing by name. Two angles are complementary if they add up to 90 degrees, and supplementary if they add up to 180 degrees. When two lines intersect, the pair of angles directly across from each other are called vertical angles, and vertical angles are always equal, since each vertical angle and its adjacent angle together form a straight line of 180 degrees, forcing both vertical angles to share whatever is left over after subtracting that same adjacent angle.

A more involved and heavily tested setup is two parallel lines cut by a third line called a transversal. This creates eight angles total, four at each intersection, and they fall into predictable relationships. Corresponding angles, the ones in matching positions at each intersection, are equal. Alternate interior angles, the ones between the two parallel lines but on opposite sides of the transversal, are equal. Alternate exterior angles, the ones outside the two parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal, are equal. Co-interior angles, also called same-side interior angles, sit between the parallel lines on the same side of the transversal, and rather than being equal, they are supplementary, adding to 180 degrees.

Beyond angles, lines are also described by their slope, a number measuring steepness as rise over run, the change in y divided by the change in x between any two points on the line. Slope connects two lines to each other in two useful ways: parallel lines always have equal slopes, since they rise and run at exactly the same rate, and perpendicular lines always have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, meaning their product is -1.

Suppose two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and one of the resulting angles measures 65 degrees. The angle in the corresponding position at the other intersection also measures 65 degrees, by the corresponding angles relationship. The alternate interior angle, positioned between the parallel lines on the opposite side of the transversal, also measures 65 degrees. The co-interior angle on the same side of the transversal, however, is supplementary to the 65 degree angle rather than equal to it, so it measures 180 minus 65, which is 115 degrees. As a check, that 65 degree angle and its 115 degree co-interior partner should add to 180, and 65 + 115 does equal 180.

Now find the slope of the line through the points (2, 3) and (6, 11). Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x: (11 - 3)/(6 - 2), which is 8/4, or 2. A line perpendicular to this one must have a slope that is the negative reciprocal of 2, which is -1/2, and you can verify that relationship because 2 times -1/2 equals -1, matching the perpendicular slope rule.

These angle relationships are the foundation for the next chapter, since the fact that a straight line measures 180 degrees is exactly what explains why the three angles inside a triangle always add up to 180 degrees as well.
